I am 64 years old and have farmed this land in Quzhou County all my life. I never went to school, but I know every mu of my field and what it needs. This year, like every year, I will plant winter wheat and summer maize in rotation. That is what our land and water here on the North China Plain are made for. I have 5 mu of good farmland. I do not chase new fancy crops — wheat and maize have never failed me, and the grain station buys them at steady prices.

For the winter wheat, I will sow an improved variety in late September or early October. I will rotary-till the soil first to break up the stubble and prepare a fine seedbed. I will apply compound fertilizer as basal dressing and top-dress with urea in spring when the wheat turns green. The wheat needs four good irrigations: the winter irrigation to keep it safe from frost, the green-turn irrigation, the jointing irrigation, and one at grain filling. I will spray pesticides four times to keep away aphids, rust, and weeds.

As soon as the wheat is harvested in early June, I will plant summer maize directly without tillage — there is no time to waste because the maize growing season is short. I will use a hybrid variety like Nongda 372, which yields well and resists lodging. The maize will get two irrigations, one at the jointing stage and one at flowering, and I will spray pesticides three times for borers and weeds. I have learned that saving labor on tillage for maize is wise — the soil keeps its moisture better, and I can get the crop in quickly.

decision.reasoning_summary: I have farmed these 5 mu in Quzhou County for decades, and the wheat-maize double-cropping system is the only reliable way to feed my family and earn cash. Wheat is rotary-tilled and heavily irrigated because it grows through the dry season, while maize is no-till planted immediately after wheat harvest to catch the summer rains and heat. I use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed, apply moderate fertilizers, and spray regularly to protect yields.
